‘THERE IS NO ARAB AMERICA’ — She Just Said What Millions Were Thinking. Do You Agree With Her?

A massive national debate has erupted after newly elected Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed declared Michigan the "capital of Arab America" during a speech in Washington, D.C.

Turning Point USA CEO Erika Kirk fired back immediately with a response that is setting the internet on fire —

"There is no 'Arab America.' There is only the United States of America." — Erika Kirk

The controversy centers on two opposing views of the country —

Abdul El-Sayed celebrated his historic Senate victory by calling his home state the heart of Arab America.

 Erika Kirk argued that dividing the country into separate cultural sub-nations undermines unity under one American flag.

 Supporters on both sides are clashing across every social platform in one of the most heated debates of the year.

Did she say what needed to be said, or was she out of line?

Sgt Daniel Gurr
Died: August 5, 2011

21, of Vernal, Utah; assigned to 3rd Reconnaissance Battalion, 3rd Marine Division, II Marine Expeditionary Force (Forward), Okinawa, Japan; died Aug. 5 in Helmand province, Afghanistan, while conducting combat operations.

From The Vernal Express 8/9/2011

Sgt. Daniel David Gurr USMC was taken back to the loving arms of his Heavenly Father on Aug. 5, 2011. He was killed while defending his country in Afghanistan.

Daniel was born March 17, 1990 to David and Tracy Gurr. He was the second of four children. Daniel graduated from Uintah High School in 2008 where served as a member of his Junior Class Presidency. He participated in football, was the captain of his soccer team and was named as an All American. During his senior year he joined the Marine Corps which had been his lifelong ambition.

Daniel was full of life! His smile would brighten any room that he walked into, he brought joy to everyone he met. Anything that he did was done with all the energy and enthusiasm he had. Daniel enjoyed doing most anything, camping, hunting, fishing, riding four-wheelers and snowboarding, but most of all he enjoyed stirring up excitement while hanging out with family and friends.

Daniel had always wanted to be a Marine. He wanted to be the best and poured his heart and soul into his career. His great-grandfather AA (Mac) McCarrel was a veteran of World War II who had fought in the South Pacific was Daniel’s hero and Daniel was Mac’s. He was very proud of him. Daniel is and always will be our hero! He will greatly missed by all who knew him.

Daniel is survived by his mother, Tracy Beede; father, David (Dana) Gurr; sisters, Ashley (Shane) Mecham and Caitlyn Gurr; brother, Austin Gurr; and nephew, Karsyn Gurr; numerous step brothers and step sister; maternal grandparents, Georgia and Mike Vander Linden (Vernal); Dean and Connie Abplanalp (Florida); paternal grandparents, Gen and Janet Gurr (Vernal); many great-grandparents; aunts; uncles and cousins; his high school sweetheart Stephanie Sabin; and his Marine brothers in 3rd Reconnaissance Battalion, 3rd Marine Division. Daniel was preceded in death by his great grandparents AA (Mac) and Adoree McCarrel and great-grandfather Earl Gurr.

FLORIDA LEARJET DISASTER  NTSB Recovers Cockpit Voice Recorder From Deep Crater. Will The Audio Reveal What Happened?

Federal investigators with the NTSB have officially recovered the cockpit voice recorder from the Learjet 60 that crashed near Greenacres, Florida, claiming the lives of all nine people on board.

The heavily damaged orange recorder was unearthed from the impact crater and immediately flown to the agency's specialized Vehicle Recorders Laboratory in Washington, D.C., where audio engineers are working to extract the final minutes of crew conversations.

Key investigation updates confirmed by federal officials —

Excavation Completed — Search crews have wrapped up excavation work at the primary impact crater near Greenacres after recovering the flight recorder and engine components reported by CNN.

Crucial Audio Evidence — Specialized engineers in Washington, D.C. are evaluating whether the battered unit's memory modules survived the extreme impact to provide cockpit communications and flight deck warnings.

Debris Field Clues — Investigators previously documented that parts of the jet's left elevator separated in flight between 1.3 and 3.8 miles before the aircraft entered its fatal vertical descent, according to tracking data on Flightradar24.

What do you think caused this catastrophic descent — mechanical failure, severe turbulence, or an in-flight breakup?

The U.S. Army has officially given its culinary specialists a battlefield rebrand, formally redesignating soldiers holding the 92G military occupational specialty as “tactical field feeding specialists.”

The title change was officially approved by Headquarters, Department of the Army G-1 and unveiled during a redesignation ceremony hosted by the Quartermaster School at Fort Gregg-Adams.

The Army first established food service specialists under the 94B identifier in the 1960s before transitioning the MOS to 92G Culinary Specialist in 1995. Now, service leaders say the latest rebrand reflects a strategic shift away from routine garrison dining facilities toward large-scale combat operations in austere, contested environments.

With the military increasingly privatizing installation dining facilities, 92Gs are being realigned toward mobile kitchen trailers, assault feeding systems, and expeditionary containerized kitchens designed to sustain troops on dispersed frontlines.

Naturally, the grandiose new job title has sparked endless humor across the ranks, with troops joking about high-speed combat spatulas, tactical ladle deployments, and operator-grade scrambled eggs.

Yet Army leadership stands by the change, emphasizing that sustained frontline combat power requires agile logistical feeding capable of operating under fire.

Does rebranding Army cooks as tactical field feeders reflect genuine battlefield modernization, or is it classic military bureaucracy at work?

#USArmy #MilitaryLife #92G

Under the Justice for Citizens Wrongfully Detained by ICE Act, introduced in Congress by Representative Teresa Leger Fernández, U.S. citizens who are unlawfully arrested or detained by federal immigration officers without a warrant or probable cause would receive an express right to sue in federal court. If successful, the legislation mandates a minimum statutory payout of $500,000 for the initial detention, with an additional $100,000 awarded for every subsequent day spent behind bars. Crucially, the bill strips officers of qualified immunity and waives the federal government’s sovereign immunity defenses, removing the legal shield that historically derailed wrongful arrest lawsuits.

The legislative push follows a wave of high-profile incidents and investigative reports, including findings cited by Newsweek revealing that more than 500 American citizens have been stopped, questioned, or held at gunpoint during aggressive immigration operations since early 2025. Civil rights organizations and groups like LULAC argue that without severe financial penalties, federal paramilitaries will continue operating on a "grab first, justify later" mentality that routinely violates Fourth Amendment protections based on skin tone and language.

The Department of Homeland Security and conservative lawmakers have mounted fierce opposition, warning that six-figure automatic bounties would undermine frontline law enforcement, expose agents to personal legal harassment, and incentivize political activists to deliberately obstruct lawful enforcement sweeps against dangerous criminal aliens.

Should taxpayers automatically pay six-figure damages to citizens caught in immigration sweeps to deter federal overreach, or does stripping officer immunity handcuff agents tasked with securing the homeland?

Marine Staff Sgt. Patrick R. Dolphin
Died July 31, 2011 Serving During Operation Enduring Freedom

CAMP LEATHERNECK, Afghanistan (Oct. 3, 2010) - As bullets whizzed past, Gunnery Sgt. Eric J. Fears knew one thing; he had to continue with the mission even though two of his Marines had just been killed by an improvised explosive device. He showed his Marines that they had to keep fighting, and they did. 

On Oct. 3, Fears was presented with a Bronze Star Medal with Combat Distinguishing Device for his heroic actions on that day in Jan. 2009 as a squad leader with 3d Battalion, 8th Marine Regiment in support of Operation Enduring Freedom.

After the deadly IED attack, Fears managed to stay calm and focused despite being under heavy small arms fire and indirect fire from an entrenched enemy. The mission at hand and recovering the bodies of his two men became his focus.

“Two of my Marines were hit with an IED,” said Fears, now the staff non-commissioned officer in charge of Bridge Platoon, Alpha Company, 9th Engineer Support Battalion, 1st Marine Logistics Group (Forward). “We were taking a lot of fire, but we made sure to get them back.”

Fears encouraged his Marines to keep fighting even though they lost two of their own. Through his courage, he set the example for his Marines.
“On that day, he showed his Marines it takes good leadership and a lot of courage to continue on with the mission,” said First Sgt. Lawrence D. Wei, the Alpha Co. first sergeant with 9th ESB, 1st MLG (FWD).

Fears is a strong leader who adds a great amount of skill to the Marines of 9th ESB through his vast experience and knowledge.

“He's experienced,” said Wei. “He has had seven deployments, and he has been in division and now he's in MLG. You don't really find all the qualifications he has in everyone.”

Fears' solid character, which makes him successful in the Marine Corps, does not go unnoticed by those he serves under.

“He's very calm, patient and firm,” said Wei. “Everything that makes him a good Marine was required of him that day.”

Fears accepted the award, but passed the credit to his Marines.

“I'm honored, very honored,” said Fears from Blue Ridge, Ga., “I earned this for when I was attached to 3/8, and my Marines were on the front lines and were finding a lot of IEDs. I wear this Bronze Star not just for myself, but all the engineers that were with me at the time.”

You now have to show a government ID to buy workout powder, but you can cast an election ballot with zero identification.

Starting January 1, 2027, buyers in California will legally have to present a photo ID and undergo age verification just to purchase over-the-counter creatine and workout supplements. Lawmakers pushed the bill through under the banner of protecting teenagers from body dysmorphia and unregulated muscle powders.

Yet across the country, millions of Americans are looking at the contrast in utter disbelief. While buying a tub of basic fitness powder now requires official identification, legislation simultaneously prevents polling locations from requiring voters to show an ID before casting a ballot in elections.

To many, it represents the complete inversion of common sense — treating an over-the-counter amino acid with stricter federal-style security than the sacred democratic vote that decides the leadership of the free world.

Does requiring an ID for workout supplements while banning voter ID at the polls prove our national priorities are completely broken, or are public health restrictions for minors entirely separate from constitutional voting rights?

Drop your thoughts below.

Are America’s most elite helicopter pilots lowering their legendary standards to survive a military-wide pilot drought?

In a stunning announcement that sent shockwaves through Army aviation, Army Special Operations Command revealed that pilots no longer need a minimum number of flight hours as a pilot-in-command to apply for the 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment. For decades, the Night Stalkers required at least 50 pilot-in-command hours and 500 total flight hours — with applicants during the Global War on Terror routinely stacking hundreds more before daring to try out.

Now, that foundational requirement has been wiped away.

The move is the starkest symptom yet of a deep crisis across military rotary-wing aviation. Aggressive commercial airline recruitment has drained the Army of thousands of seasoned warrant officers, peacetime flight hour budgets have steadily plummeted, and the Pentagon is divesting hundreds of manned helicopters to fund uncrewed drone swarms. With conventional aviation units flying fewer hours than ever, younger pilots simply cannot log the cockpit time once needed to qualify for special ops assessment.

While USASOC insists its brutal Green Platoon and multi-year internal training pipeline will protect frontline lethality, veteran aviators are sounding the alarm that the military’s talent reservoir is rapidly running dry.

Does dropping entry requirements allow special ops to build great pilots from the ground up, or is America’s most elite aviation unit being forced to compromise standards due to systemic military neglect?

Capt. Lindsay Gordon Heisler, West Point Class of 2012, received the 2019 Alexander Nininger Award for Valor at Arms presented by the West Point Association of Graduates.

She received the award for actions on Dec. 5, 2015, when she was serving as a co-pilot/gunner of an AH-64 Apache helicopter in Afghanistan. She and her co-pilot's actions allowed a ranger unit to be extracted from a firefight near the border between Afghanistan and Pakistan.

In addition to the Distinguished Flying Cross, Heisler has been awarded two Air Medals, the Army Commendation Medal with oak leaf cluster, the Army Achievement Medal with oak leaf cluster, the Combat Action Badge, the Aviator Badge, and the Air Assault Badge.

A London judge just sentenced Russell Brand to 10.5 years in prison, bringing a sudden end to years of public defiance.

The 51-year-old comedian and online commentator was convicted at Southwark Crown Court on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault involving four women between 2004 and 2009, concluding a weeks-long criminal trial that gripped the United Kingdom.

During the proceedings, prosecutors detailed predatory behavior during the peak of Brand’s mainstream television and radio fame, describing his actions as ruthless and manipulative. Under English sentencing guidelines, Brand must serve at least two-thirds of his sentence behind bars before becoming eligible for parole consideration.

Brand, who had pleaded not guilty to all charges and maintained that all encounters were consensual, built a massive alternative media following in recent years centered on spirituality, wellness, and anti-establishment commentary. The verdict and heavy prison term mark a catastrophic collapse for a figure who once commanded Hollywood box offices and millions of online subscribers.

Does this landmark verdict deliver necessary justice and long-overdue accountability for victims, or does the multi-year delay and intense media spectacle show that high-profile celebrity figures face an impossible standard in the court of public opinion?

Drop your thoughts below.

Part of the Soldier’s Creed is never to leave behind a fallen comrade. On the night of March 13, 2006, then-Sgt. Wilzcek, Sgt. Row, then-Pfc. Alvarez, then-Pfc. Pushkin and the rest of their squad risked life and limb to live up to that promise.

Row, the point man, was leading the soldiers through dark, narrow alleys in the city of Ramadi as the squad headed back to base. Suddenly, two men darted into a nearby house, and at that hour, Row saw that as a clear sign of imminent danger. He stopped the team, but within seconds the street exploded with an onslaught of machine-gun and small-arms fire, RPG explosions, and hand grenades. The squad dropped to the ground and directed fire at the enemy’s position.

Alvarez moved to a covered position to reload his weapon, and he noticed one of his comrades had been hit and was lying in the middle of the firefight. Without hesitation, Alvarez rushed into the kill zone to check the soldier’s vital signs – but it was too late. He covered the soldier’s body with his own and continued firing on the enemy. When he ran out of ammunition, Alvarez stood up and started dragging the soldier out of the line of fire. Row, who was pinned down nearby, provided cover fire as Alvarez struggled to move the body. When Wilzcek and Pushkin saw Alvarez’s difficulties, they ran into the open to help. But as the three moved back toward cover, two RPGs exploded 10 meters away, knocking them down and sending a volley of shrapnel into Alvarez’s right knee. The men stood up and continued dragging their comrade to the safety of a nearby courtyard.

After establishing a safe area for the injured, Pushkin and Wilzcek ran back and forth several times from the courtyard into the line of fire to rescue trapped soldiers. Meanwhile, the RPG explosions had also injured Row’s elbow with shrapnel. Even so, he continued firing on the enemy position to help the others reach safety. Once everyone was clear, Row, who was alone in the middle of the street, called for help. As Row remembered later, “I was trapped in the street, and [Pushkin and Wilzcek] pulled me out of there.”

The squad was now in the courtyard, and medical assistance was being administered – but their work was not done: enemy fire continued to light up the area. When the squad started planning the next phase, Alvarez refused to be moved with the other injured soldiers, staying to help in the fight.

The insurgents, seeing the evacuation in progress, focused their fire on the rescuers. Wilzcek, already on the roof, began firing back. After clearing the rooms below, Pushkin and his team hurried up to the roof to help Wilzcek. Row grabbed a Bunker Defeat Munition – a shoulder-launched explosive for use against fortified positions – but his injured elbow prevented him from using it. He ran up to the roof, handed the weapon to Pushkin, and helped guide Pushkin toward the targets. With Row and Wilzcek providing cover fire, Pushkin took aim and fired, destroying the enemy’s position and killing a number of insurgents. With that, the squad was able to leave the area safely.

He possesses one of the most impeccably polished resumes in modern American political history, yet his road to the Oval Office faces a fierce ideological battlefield.

Pete Buttigieg’s trajectory reads like an intentional blueprint for the presidency. A Phi Beta Kappa graduate of Harvard University, a Rhodes Scholar at Oxford, and a self-taught polyglot capable of speaking multiple languages, he stepped away from private sector consulting to commission as a naval intelligence officer in the U.S. Navy Reserve. In 2014, while serving as mayor of South Bend, Indiana, he deployed to Afghanistan for seven months, conducting counterterrorism armed reconnaissance and convoy driving through hostile territory. Rising from small-town mayor to a breakout primary contender and ultimately serving as Secretary of Transportation, he established a reputation as one of his party’s most disciplined and formidable communicators, regularly stepping into adversarial media environments to debate conservative hosts.

As the political landscape pivots toward the 2028 presidential campaign, Buttigieg stands near the top of nearly every prospective Democratic shortlist. Supporters argue that his calm debate demeanor, executive cabinet stewardship, Midwestern roots, and combat veteran credentials make him the rare unifying figure capable of appealing to suburban moderates and traditional defense voters alike.

However, detractors from both sides of the political aisle present sharp counterarguments. Critics on the right point to supply chain logjams, airline travel meltdowns, and regulatory controversies during his tenure at the Department of Transportation, while skeptics on the progressive left argue that his technocratic style and corporate background fail to resonate with blue-collar workers demanding a disruptive economic overhaul.

Does Pete Buttigieg’s rare combination of military service, academic pedigree, and polished communication make him the ideal future commander-in-chief, or does his technocratic track record feel out of touch with the raw economic realities facing middle-class Americans?

#PeteButtigieg #2028Election #Politics

Starting January 1, 2027, high school athletes across California will no longer be able to walk into a nutrition shop or order a tub of creatine online without flashing a government ID.

Under Assembly Bill 2030, signed into law by Governor Gavin Newsom, California has enacted sweeping restrictions prohibiting the sale of over-the-counter dietary supplements marketed for weight loss or muscle building to anyone under the age of 18. While legislative sponsors argue the statute is vital to shield teenagers from predatory marketing, eating disorders, and unregulated diet pills, the law explicitly flags creatine alongside weight-loss botanical extracts, triggering fierce pushback from fitness enthusiasts, sports scientists, and trade groups like the Council for Responsible Nutrition.

The new regulations place significant compliance hurdles on retailers and delivery services alike. Brick-and-mortar storefronts must mandate physical age checks for anyone who does not appear over 18, and stores are encouraged to place covered products behind counters or in locked display cases. Remote sellers face even steeper barriers, requiring third-party database identity verification during checkout followed by mandatory adult signatures and photo ID inspections upon parcel delivery, with violations carrying civil penalties of up to $1,000 per infraction.

Critics in the sports nutrition community point out that creatine monohydrate is one of the most exhaustively studied, safe, and naturally occurring nutritional compounds in human biology, widely recognized for enhancing cellular energy and cognitive health without hormonal interference. By grouping essential sports nutrition in the same regulatory bucket as dangerous diet pills, opponents argue the state is overreaching into the training routines of responsible young athletes.

Does regulating basic workout supplements like creatine protect teen health, or is this an unnecessary case of state overreach into youth athletics?

#California #Fitness #GavinNewsom

3,800 meters. 2.36 miles. 12,467 feet.

A bullet took nearly nine full seconds in flight before striking its target—shattering the confirmed world record for the longest sniper kill in human history.

The shot was made by 58-year-old Ukrainian SBU counter-intelligence sniper Viacheslav Kovalskyi and his spotter across the Dnipro River in the Kherson region.

At a distance of over 41 football fields, hitting a human-sized target defies conventional ballistic physics:

The Coriolis Effect: Because the bullet stayed airborne for nearly nine seconds, the sniper team had to calculate the physical rotation of the Earth beneath the projectile.

Massive Bullet Drop: The bullet dropped over 300 feet (100+ meters) from apex to impact, requiring the shooter to angle the rifle high into the sky like an artillery piece.

Shifting Winds: Factoring in temperature, barometric air pressure, humidity, and varying crosswinds across two miles of open water and terrain.

The hardware behind the shot was just as extreme: the custom "Horizon's Lord" (Volodar Obriyu) anti-materiel precision rifle, measuring over six feet in length.

In the bottom of the photo, you can see why this rifle reaches where standard weapons fail:

On the right is a standard .50 BMG (12.7x99mm) round.

On the left is the monster 12.7x114mm HL cartridge—a massive 14.5mm anti-aircraft casing necked down to fire a heavy .50-caliber precision match bullet at over 3,400 feet per second, keeping the projectile supersonic far past two miles.

The shot surpassed the previous world record held by a Canadian JTF-2 sniper in Iraq (3,540 meters) and pushed the outer limits of extreme long-range shooting.

To our long-range shooters and snipers: factoring in a 9-second flight time, the Coriolis effect, and crosswinds across 2.36 miles—how much of this shot was pure mathematical mastery, and how much was divine luck?

Staff Sgt. Abrahamson was deployed to Kirkuk Regional Air Base in Iraq to support counterinsurgent missions in the area.

From Jan. 22 to June 5, 2006, Abrahamson assisted with several successful operations, including overseeing the safety and workload of 16,000 Coalition forces, multinational contractors, and local Iraqis.

During that time, Abrahamson managed more than 150 combat missions within a 68,000 square-mile area under the constant threat of insurgent attacks. These missions allowed Coalition forces to find and destroy deadly IEDs and weapons caches.

While supporting one combat team, Abrahamson found and destroyed 70 IEDs placed along vital supply routes connecting cities in northern Iraq. For his work, Abrahamson received the Bronze Star on Jan. 24, 2007.

“IF YOU ARE COMING IN HERE WITH SORROW, GO ELSEWHERE. I AM GOING TO MAKE A FULL RECOVERY.” — Navy SEAL Jason Redman on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the most inspirational conversations in the history of The Shawn Ryan Show (Episode #032), wounded Navy SEAL Lieutenant Jason Redman recounted the 2007 ambush outside Fallujah where he was struck by eight rounds including heavy machine-gun fire that shattered his arm and tore away half his face and the legendary sign he taped to his hospital door.

In his own words:

“When I woke up at Bethesda, my face was rebuilt with metal plates, my jaw was wired shut, and my arm was completely shredded.

People would walk into my hospital room family members, friends, senior officers and the moment they looked at me, their faces would melt into pure horror and grief. They would start crying, sobbing, looking at me with this sickening pity, as if my life was completely over.

That look made me sick to my stomach. I was alive. My guys were alive.

I grabbed a bright orange poster board and a black Sharpie, and with my one good hand, I wrote a sign and taped it directly to the front door of my hospital room:

 If you are coming into this room with sorrow or to feel sorry for my wounds, go elsewhere. The wounds I received I got in a job I love, doing it for people I love, supporting the freedom of a country I deeply love. I am incredibly tough and will make a full recovery. If you are not prepared for that, go elsewhere. But if you are, welcome to my room.’

That sign became our line in the sand. You don’t get to mourn me while I’m still standing.”

Jason Redman endured 37 surgeries, extensive facial reconstruction, and years of physical therapy, going on to write The Trident and Overcome and dedicating his life to helping combat veterans conquer their own life ambushes.

Banning pity from your hospital room while your jaw is wired shut and your face is held together with titanium plates is the ultimate definition of the warrior mindset.

Drop a salute in the comments for Navy SEAL Jason Redman.

Following bruising losses in the congressional midterms, conservative entrepreneur and former Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback sparked fierce debate across the right with a viral message addressing the party's future.

Fishback argued that any realistic path back to political majorities requires an immediate break from overseas military interventions and unquestioned political deference. Laying out a three-part blueprint centered on staying out of the Middle East, championing the domestic middle class, and strictly defending the Constitution, he contended that authentic populism must put domestic economic survival ahead of foreign defense spending and personality-driven loyalty.

Can the Republican coalition successfully pivot toward a non-interventionist, middle-class platform, or is the party's foreign policy consensus too deeply entrenched?

“DOZENS OF U.S. AIR FORCE REFUELING TANKERS MASS AT ISRAEL’S RAMON AIRPORT: WHAT ARE THEY PREPARING FOR?”

Striking new imagery from southern Israel shows a massive flight line of U.S. Air Force Boeing KC-135 Stratotankers staged wingtip to wingtip at Ramon Airport near Eilat.

While fighter jets and air defense batteries draw the headlines, military strategists know that aerial refueling tankers are the true operational backbone of modern air warfare. Without them, deep-penetration strikes and continuous combat air patrols are impossible.

Key strategic insights behind the heavy tanker buildup:

The Ultimate Force-Multiplier: Fighters like the F-35 Lightning II, F-15E Strike Eagle, and Israeli F-35I Adir carry limited internal fuel. Staging dozens of heavy tankers provides the aerial gas stations required to execute and sustain multi-wave, long-range strikes over 1,000 miles from base.

Why Ramon Airport?: Located in the Timna Valley near Eilat, Ramon Airport offers a massive 11,800-foot runway and expansive apron space, allowing U.S. heavy strategic aircraft to stage outside congested IDF bases like Nevatim while opening direct flight corridors over the Red Sea and Gulf.

Deterrence in Plain Sight: Assembling this volume of refueling capacity in broad daylight sends an unmistakable deterrent signal to regional adversaries that coalition airpower can stay airborne indefinitely.

Round-the-Clock Air Defense: In addition to offensive strike support, continuous tanker rotations allow interceptors to maintain 24/7 loitering orbits to shoot down inbound ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and one-way attack drones.

Do you see this buildup as preparation for imminent joint strikes, or is it a massive display of force designed to deter wider regional conflict?

November 2004, Fallujah, Iraq. A gunner from 1st Battalion, 8th Marine Regiment (1/8) lines up a shot with a Mk 153 Mod 0 Shoulder-Launched Multipurpose Assault Weapon (SMAW) while a fellow Marine provides security with an M16A4 during the height of Operation Phantom Fury.

The Second Battle of Fallujah remains the heaviest, bloodiest urban combat the Marine Corps had faced since the Battle of Hue City in 1968. As infantrymen cleared city blocks fortified with sandbagged machine-gun nests, reinforced concrete sniper hides, and booby-trapped courtyards, the SMAW was an indispensable "wall-buster."

Fitted with an integrated 9mm spotting rifle on the side of the tube, the gunner could fire ballistically matched tracer rounds to verify his point of aim before sending an 83mm High-Explosive Dual-Purpose (HEDP) or newly fielded Novel Explosive (NE thermobaric) rocket straight through exterior masonry, breaching fortified structures and neutralizing hostile strongpoints from the street.

To anyone who fought in the streets of Fallujah or humped a SMAW on deployment: What do you remember most about the raw concussive blast of that rocket? Sound off below.

On August 3, 2026, 255 days into an exhausting marathon deployment aboard the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln, 19-year-old aviation mechanic Nicholas McKelvey stepped off the ship and plunged into the Arabian Sea.
He survived 50 minutes in the open water before a search-and-rescue helicopter crew pulled him aboard. In an interview detailing his ordeal with The New York Times, McKelvey described working relentless 12-hour flight deck shifts in blistering Middle Eastern heat, enduring persistent food rationing, and missing the birth of his first child while thousands of miles from home. When asked what drove him to the edge, his answer was direct and heartbreaking — “I didn't want to be there anymore.”
Instead of receiving medical rehabilitation, McKelvey was charged under military law with malingering and unauthorized absence. Following a disciplinary hearing, the Navy handed the teenager a general discharge under honorable conditions on October 29. While avoiding a court-martial, the administrative separation strips him of his post-9/11 GI Bill education benefits, leaving his young family to finance his schooling through student loans.
The ruling has sparked fierce scrutiny over how the military handles sailors pushed to their psychological limit during extended overseas deployments. Navy policy states that suicidal ideation and suicide attempts are medical issues rather than disciplinary offenses, yet commanders retain wide discretion to pursue separate misconduct charges. Documents submitted to Congress revealed that the Abraham Lincoln operated with just six mental health professionals and five chaplains to serve more than 5,000 personnel aboard, during a deployment that saw eight separate suicide attempts across the strike group.
The Abraham Lincoln finally returned to San Diego in October after 322 days away, but Navy leaders have warned that double-pump, 11-month deployments could become the operational norm as global fleet commitments outpace ship numbers.
If you or a service member you know is struggling with mental health or thoughts of self-harm, confidential support is available 24/7 by calling or texting 988 in the United States and pressing 1.
Does discharging sailors who break down on extended deployments protect military discipline, or does it penalize young troops for systemic readiness failures?

U.S. Special Operations Command has launched a formal search for an ultra-lightweight belt-fed weapon system under its Flyweight Assault Machine Gun initiative, according to reporting by Task & Purpose.

The program aims to replace the legacy Mk 46, a special operations derivative of the M249 Squad Automatic Weapon that has served elite units for roughly three decades. According to command spokesperson Navy Cmdr. Joe Vermette, SOCOM wants a 5.56x45mm NATO machine gun that weighs approximately 10 pounds unloaded — over five pounds lighter than the Mk 46 — while incorporating a 30-second quick-change barrel, low-recoil controllability, and full compatibility with modern visual augmentation optics. The command plans to award a development contract late next year, with operational testing and fielding slated for fiscal year 2028.

Can modern engineering deliver sustained belt-fed firepower in a 10-pound package without sacrificing barrel life and thermal performance?

Pop culture gave Navy SEALs all the movies, but anyone in the military community who actually knows the pipelines will tell you: EOD School is a psychological slaughterhouse.

BUD/S tests how much raw pain your body can take before your mind gives up.

EOD School tests whether your brain can stay laser-focused when the penalty for being 99% right is catastrophic failure.

Candidates spend almost an entire year memorizing thousands of foreign ordnance schematics, complex chemical fuzes, home-made explosives chemistry, and improvised trigger circuits. You don't get to just "gut it out" on adrenaline. You have to think, calculate, and execute microscopic physical movements under crushing anxiety.

One requires you to be an absolute physical animal. The other requires you to be a calm, surgical scientist with nerves of steel.

Respect to both, but where do you stand: BUD/S or EOD School? Drop your take below.

Michael "Rod" Rodriguez was born into a legacy of warriors.

With a father who fought in Vietnam and two grandfathers who served in World War II, Rod knew his path early. Graduating high school at sixteen, he enlisted in the United States Army at seventeen, joining the 10th Mountain Division and deploying into combat in Somalia in 1993 and later to Haiti.

In 1997, he earned his Green Beret, taking on one of the most demanding specialties in the military as an 18D Special Forces Medical Sergeant and sniper with 7th Special Forces Group.

Over twenty-one years and ten combat deployments across Colombia, Panama, Peru, Bolivia, and Afghanistan, Rod repeatedly put his body on the line. He endured multiple concussions and traumatic brain injuries from enemy blast waves, hiding his symptoms because he refused to leave his teammates down a gun.

Capt. Brian Erickson, a pilot from the 75th Fighter Squadron, was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross with Valor on July 11, 2008.

Capt. Brian Erickson, 75th FS chief of mission planning, earned the medal while deployed to Bagram Air Base, Afghanistan, for providing ground alert close air support to a German Provincial Reconstruction Team that was under nighttime fire from insurgents in a valley of the Hindu-Kush mountains.

"I'm extremely impressed with the way Captain Erickson handled himself out there," said Colonel Kenneth Todorov, 23rd Wing commander, "He provided close air support in hazardous conditions, with no forward air controller and led a successful mission with valor."

On Oct. 16, 2006, Captain Erickson and his wingman, who were then part of the 75th Expeditionary Fighter Squadron, received a short-notice call to provide aerial support to six German soldiers trapped between two mountain ranges. They were receiving enemy fire in the form of rocket-propelled grenades, machine guns, and small-arms fire.

Up until the call, previous flights of non-tactical aircraft had been unable to help the stranded PRT due to their location, limited communication capabilities, and lack of moonlight. Without illumination from the moon or another source, the pilots' night vision goggles provided little assistance.

Once he arrived on scene, Captain Erickson determined there was room for only one aircraft above the mountain tops and just below the clouds. He assigned the safe altitude above the clouds to his wingman, who searched for the insurgents' location with his advanced targeting pod and night vision goggles.

As Captain Erickson flew his A-10 deep into the moonless valley, where the only light on the ground was from insurgent weapons fire, his wingman flew above to relay reports about where the weapon bursts were coming from. Before Capt. Erickson could employ any of his own weapons, he needed to determine the exact location of the PRT to avoid friendly fire.

"I initially had my infrared sensor on to pinpoint the location of the insurgents. The problem with using the infrared was that every time a rocket-propelled grenade went off, the glow impeded my ability to navigate the dark canyon. The whole screen would go white, and I couldn't see outside my cockpit. The only solution was to turn the screens off," said Captain Erickson.

After Captain Erickson turned off his infrared sensor, he continued his low-level runs in search of the PRT. This proved an even more difficult task because the PRT's signaling device, an infrared strobe, was malfunctioning, and the German soldiers, who were untrained in communicating with aircraft, continued to take harassing enemy fire. The chaos of the situation was impaired even more by the PRT's limited proficiency in English. These limitations in combination with the enemy fire caused the PRT to provide confusing information on their exact location.

Realizing that time was running out for the PRT, Captain Erickson released a series of covert illumination flares only visible through night vision devices. Able to "see", he used geographic references from the air and ground to narrow down the PRT's location. During this time, the captain and his wingman were able to identify a location where they believed the enemy fire was coming from.

To be sure of the PRT's location, Captain Erickson conducted a low-altitude show-of-force. He flew between the enemy and friendly positions at 2,000 feet and deployed pyrotechnic self-protection flares, which lit the night sky. His hope was that the enemy would alert to his position and break their attack on the PRT long enough for his wingman to search for clues of the enemy's exact position.

"After we located where we thought the insurgents were, I had my wingman light-up the area with his targeting pod," said Captain Erickson. "During this time the weapons-fire against the Germans was also becoming increasingly accurate, and the need to bring the situation to a close was becoming more-and-more imperative. After we were able to determine that we were, in fact, targeting the insurgents and not the pinned-down German PRT team, it was time to take action."

With Captain Erickson's wingman marking the enemy's position with his TGP's infrared pointer, the PRT confirmed the mark as the enemy fire point of origin. In a single pass, Captain Erickson employed 240 30-millimeter rounds from the aircraft's GAU-8 cannon. This completely halted the enemy's fire and saved the lives of six German soldiers.

Captain Erickson and his wingman remained in the area to monitor both the friendly and enemy positions until the Iraqi National Police and International Security Assistance Force Quick Reaction Force were able to reach and recover the PRT and bring them to safety.

Captain Erickson credited the operation's success to his training. Although he was honored to receive the Distinguished Flying Cross with Valor for "doing the job he's trained to do," he pointed out a higher honor.

"The real reward was returning those six coalition soldiers safely to the village they were working at as part of the PRT team," said Captain Erickson.

His quick thinking and aggressive actions were crucial in saving the lives of two of the three casualties.

On May 26, 2008, during a high-stakes daylight direct-action raid against an insurgent compound in Paktya Province, Afghanistan, Army Rangers from the 2nd Battalion, 75th Ranger Regiment found themselves locked in a point-blank firefight. Refusing to stay down, Petry dragged himself to cover behind a small courtyard structure alongside two wounded comrades, Specialist Daniel Higgins and Private First Class Lucas Robinson. As insurgent fighters maneuvered to close range, an enemy stick grenade sailed over the wall, landing just feet away from the trapped, wounded Rangers.

With only two seconds before detonation, Petry did not hesitate. Despite bullets tearing through both thighs, he lunged forward toward the explosive, gripped the live grenade in his bare right hand, and hurled it away from his men. The grenade detonated the instant it cleared his grip, severing his right hand and peppering his body with shrapnel.

Petry immediately placed a tourniquet on his own severed wrist, keyed his radio, and calmly continued reporting enemy positions and directing the fight until backup arrived. His instantaneous decision saved both of his fellow Rangers from fatal blast wounds, earning him the Medal of Honor.

Then Cpl. Adams and his squad were traveling toward Husaybah, Iraq, on Jan. 6, 2005, to provide cover for a Marine reconnaissance unit that was scouting the area. As the convoy was traveling toward a roadway in the city of Husaybah dubbed the “intersection of death,” insurgents attacked, using RPGs and machine guns.

Adams’ Humvee crashed, stranding its occupants in the line of fire. Adams immediately jumped out of the vehicle and took up a safer location to help the rest of the squad return fire as other Marines worked to dislodge the Humvee.

Once the vehicle was freed, Adams and his squad began searching the area for other broken-down Humvees and injured comrades as insurgents continued their attack. They spotted a disabled Humvee and went over to help.

Suddenly, a RPG struck Adams’ vehicle, killing one Marine and injuring others. Adams was also hit – his left arm and both hands had shrapnel wounds, his right arm was broken, and he had a sprained ankle. But Adams didn’t have time to think about his injuries or the pain; he had to quickly scramble out of the burning vehicle and assess the situation.

After leading his squad to a safer location, Adams realized he was missing a Marine. Adams took off running through the line of fire, back toward the burning vehicle. He located the missing Marine and realized he had died in the attack. Grabbing his body, he ran back through the hail of enemy gunfire with the recovered Marine’s body.

Adams refused medical attention for his injuries until he and all of his Marines arrived safely back at headquarters. On April 17, 2006, Adams was awarded the Silver Star for his bravery.

Then-Spc. Gallucci and his six-member civil affairs team spent almost a year in Iraq between 2003 and 2004 helping to rebuild the infrastructure and improve the quality of life for the Iraqis.

The team worked and lived in towns near the Iranian border, performing tasks such as getting schools and municipal governments up and running, and making sure the teachers and workers were on the payroll.

In September 2005, Gallucci was awarded the Bronze Star Medal for his work.

In 1980, after the catastrophic failure of Operation Eagle Claw in the Iranian desert, the U.S. military realized it had a fatal gap: it lacked a dedicated, full-time maritime counter-terrorist assault force.

The Navy turned to a hardened, foul-mouthed Vietnam veteran who had terrorized the Viet Cong so badly in the Mekong Delta that they put a 50,000-piastre bounty on his head: Commander Richard Marcinko.

His mission: build America’s premier maritime counter-terror unit from scratch.

At the time, the Navy only had two active SEAL teams: Team One and Team Two. Marcinko intentionally named his new command SEAL Team Six—a psychological head-fake designed to convince Soviet intelligence that the U.S. had at least four other secret teams operating around the globe.

Marcinko threw out the traditional military rulebook. He hand-selected the deadliest, most aggressive operators in the Navy, gave them unlimited ammunition budgets, and pioneered high-intensity close-quarters battle (CQB) standards that defined modern hostage rescue.

He created the unit that eventually evolved into modern DEVGRU.

Later, the Pentagon tasked him with creating Red Cell—a secret unit made up of rogue SEALs whose job was to infiltrate America’s most secure naval bases and nuclear submarine facilities to expose security flaws using real-world terrorist tactics.

Marcinko broke rules, infuriated pencil-pushing admirals, and fought bureaucracy as ruthlessly as he fought enemies downrange.

He wasn’t a politician. He was a warfighter.
